title: PUC Acts to Protect Ratepayers, Guide Data Center Growth with New Large Load Tariff Framework
key_claim: The PA PUC voted 5-0 to adopt a model large-load tariff for customers over 50 MW individually or 100 MW in aggregate, requiring interconnection upgrade costs to be recovered directly from large load customers, with deposits and collateral sufficient to fully cover infrastructure upgrade costs, interconnection studies within six months, and a public interconnection queue at each utility.
frame_summary: Pennsylvania's utility regulator argues that clear statewide cost-allocation rules for data centres are needed so that customers driving new infrastructure pay for it and existing ratepayers are shielded from the costs of generational load growth.
notes: Tier 1 in-window anchor for the regulatory-conversion facet: backlash converted into binding cost-allocation architecture.

title: Ratepayer Protection Pledge
key_claim: The White House called on leading US hyperscalers and AI companies to 'build, bring, or buy' all the energy needed for their data centres and pay the full cost of energy and infrastructure; pledge signatories agree to pay for all new power delivery infrastructure upgrades, negotiate separate rate structures with utilities and state governments, and pay for capacity brought online for their data centres whether they use the electricity or not.
frame_summary: The White House argues that the data-centre boom must not raise household electricity bills and that hyperscalers should voluntarily internalise the full energy and infrastructure costs of their buildout.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6m band): canonical federal acknowledgment that ratepayer politics now conditions the AI buildout; the industry counter-move the rest of the evidence base responds to.

title: Americans Oppose AI Data Centers in Their Area
key_claim: In a March 2-18, 2026 survey of 1,000 US adults, 71% oppose construction of an AI data centre in their local area (48% strongly); this exceeds the 53% who oppose a local nuclear power plant and the historical high of 63% for nuclear opposition since 2001; majorities of all party groups oppose, with 56% of Democrats and 39% of Republicans strongly opposed; 15% of opponents cite higher utility bills.
frame_summary: Gallup argues that local opposition to AI data centres is broad, intense and bipartisan, and that overcoming it now stands as a major hurdle to the expansion of AI computing and a likely campaign issue in 2026 state and local elections.
verbatim_quote: Overcoming this opposition stands as a major hurdle in the expansion of AI computing.
notes: First Gallup measurement of the question; the nuclear comparison is the load-bearing quantification anchor. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page at fetch time (2026-07-04T00:16:54Z). title: How States Are Requiring Data Centers to Pay for Grid Expansion (Comparing Ratepayer Protection Bills Across Five States)
key_claim: About one-third of enacted data-centre energy legislation this biennium includes ratepayer-protection requirements obliging data centres to fully fund their energy demand and related grid buildout; enacted laws compared span Alabama (SB 270, 150 MW threshold), Tennessee (HB 1847, 50 MW), South Dakota (SB 135, 10 MW), Nebraska (LB 1010, 20 MW) and Florida (SB 484, 50 MW), with thresholds ranging from 10 MW to 150 MW.
frame_summary: MultiState argues that ratepayer-protection legislation making data centres pay their own grid costs is the clear trend leader in state data-centre policy and will proliferate, with wide state-by-state variation that complicates compliance.
notes: Documents that the backlash has already crossed from bills into enacted law in at least five states.

title: How much is the US spending on building data centers?
key_claim: As of January 2026, US spending on data-centre construction was over $2.4 billion per month (constant 2021 dollars), roughly 16 times the level in early 2014, and has nearly tripled since AI chatbots became popular in late 2022; based on US Census Bureau construction spending data, covering physical structures only.
frame_summary: Our World in Data argues, from Census Bureau data, that US data-centre construction spending has grown extraordinarily fast and continues at record monthly levels.
verbatim_quote: roughly 16 times the level in early 2014

title: Exclusive: Local Opposition to Data Centers Explodes in 2026
key_claim: At least 20 proposed data-centre projects were cancelled after local pushback in Q1 2026, a quarterly record, representing more than $41.7 billion in investment and at least 3.5 GW of electricity demand; Heatmap Pro researchers added roughly 100 new data-centre fights to their database in three months, and at least $85 billion in projects have been cancelled over the past three years; the largest Q1 cancellation was the 1 GW Project Jarvis campus near Port St. Lucie, Florida.
frame_summary: Heatmap argues that the local backlash against data centres has not yet peaked and that cancellations are accelerating, with 2026 on track to break the annual record only months into the year.
notes: Metered site but full article text was retrieved and verified at fetch time.

title: Data center opponents have blocked or delayed projects worth nearly $130 billion in 2026, study finds
key_claim: A Data Center Watch (10a Labs) study found opponents blocked or delayed at least 75 data-centre projects worth about $130 billion in January-March 2026, the most in any three-month period since tracking began in 2023 and roughly matching all of 2025; active grassroots opposition groups more than doubled from 396 at the end of 2025 to 833 across 49 states by March; statewide moratorium proposals were introduced in 14 states, none enacted, with Maine's governor vetoing one in April; more than 300 state bills were introduced in the first six weeks of 2026.
frame_summary: NBC News, reporting the Data Center Watch study, argues that data-centre opposition has reached record scale and organisational maturity, and that leaders in both parties are recalibrating their approach to the buildout.
verbatim_quote: a structural shift rather than a cyclical spike
